The city opened a lost-and-found office for things that had never existed.

It began as a clerical error. Someone printed **LOST: ONE POSSIBLE FUTURE** on a municipal form, and because the form had all the proper boxes, the city was obliged to process it.

By Thursday, there was a queue.

A woman came looking for the bakery she would have opened if her father hadn’t fallen ill. She described the green tiles behind the counter, the bell on the door, the particular loaf she had meant to name after him.

The clerk checked the shelves.

“We have the bell,” he said.

She took it home wrapped in newspaper.

A man asked for the person he might have become if he had learned to swim. The clerk explained that they couldn’t store people.

“Against the fire code?”

“Among other things.”

They found him a towel, still warm from a summer afternoon in 1983.

Not everything could be located. Whole careers were missing. So were several marriages and a remarkably specific revolution. The office had plenty of speeches, but almost none of the courage required to deliver them.

The clerk was patient. He had worked for the city for twenty-six years. Before this, he had issued parking permits.

One evening, just before closing, a little girl arrived carrying a cardboard box.

“I think this belongs here.”

Inside was an ordinary stone.

“What was it going to be?” the clerk asked.

“A moon.”

He examined it carefully.

“For what?”

She looked at him with the exhausted tolerance children reserve for adults who ask unnecessary questions.

“For the sky.”

Of course. He filled out an intake slip.

After she left, he put the stone on the highest shelf. Then he finished the day’s paperwork, turned off the lights, and stood for a moment in the doorway.

There was just enough light to see the room.

He checked the windows. He checked the green exit sign.

Finally, he climbed onto his chair and held his hand above the stone.

His palm was faintly illuminated.

The next morning, he submitted a request for a larger building.
